advisory.title: Panic and unbounded allocation (OOM) in the CFB/OLE2 parser on malformed input
advisory.description:
The Compound File Binary (OLE2) parser (`src/cfb.rs`), used when reading `.xls` and `.xlsb`
workbooks and when extracting VBA projects from `.xlsx`, can panic or allocate without bound
on crafted input. Both are reachable through the public reader API (`open_workbook`,
`Xls::new`, `Xlsb::new`) on an attacker-supplied file. Impact is denial of service only — no
memory unsafety (safe Rust turns the out-of-bounds read into a bounds-checked panic).

1. **Reachable panic (out-of-bounds slice index).** The directory stream is iterated with
   `.chunks(128)`, but `Directory::from_slice` reads fixed offsets (`buf[..64]`,
   `buf[116..120]`, `buf[120..128]`) without checking the chunk length. A directory stream
   whose length is not a multiple of 128 yields a short final chunk, causing a panic
   (`range end index 64 out of range for slice of length N`). `SectorSize::Small` 64-byte
   mini sectors are a second trigger.

2. **Unbounded allocation / OOM.** The DIFAT loader grows the `difat` vector without bounding
   the number of iterations; a crafted self-referential DIFAT chain drives a multi-gigabyte
   allocation from a tiny file (a 512-byte file attempts an allocation of several gigabytes).

A consumer that parses untrusted or user-supplied spreadsheets can be crashed (thread panic,
or process abort under `panic=abort`) or driven out of memory by a small crafted file.

Fixed in calamine 0.38.0 (commit [b8ec4f0](https://github.com/tafia/calamine/commit/b8ec4f0)); the maintainer confirmed the fix in https://github.com/tafia/calamine/pull/762.

advisory.title: Invalid pointer dereference in `fmt::Pointer` impl for `Atomic` and `Shared` when the underlying pointer is invalid
advisory.description: Affected versions of `fmt::Display` dereference the underlying pointer. This causes a invalid pointer dereference e.g., when a pointer created with `Atomic::null` or `Shared::null`. `fmt::Debug` impls and pre-0.9 `fmt::Display` impls, which do not dereference pointers, are not affected by this issue.

advisory.title: Multiple timing variability issues in operations intended to be constant-time
advisory.description:
## Summary

Several operations intended to be constant-time could execute secret-dependent
branches, depending on the compiler and target CPU. These include subtraction,
zero counting, division, and Montgomery multiplication.

Additionally, `UintRef` equality could terminate at the first unequal limb,
and `BoxedMontyForm::invert` branched on whether an inverse exists.

## Impact

Applications using affected operations on secret integers may leak information
through timing or microarchitectural side channels. This includes information
about intermediate arithmetic values, matching limbs, and invertibility.

Such leakage could potentially enable recovery of cryptographic secrets.
Practical exploitability depends on the downstream algorithm, compiler, target
CPU, and an attacker's ability to observe the side channel.

## Resolution

Upgrade to v0.7.6, which removes the identified branches, updates `ctutils` to
include its constant-time fixes, and adds BINSEC-based regression checks using
`cargo checkct` for arithmetic on multiple targets.

advisory.title: NXDOMAIN accepted for an empty non-terminal that the NSEC record proves exists
advisory.description:
When an NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name, the queried name exists as an empty non-terminal (RFC 8020 section 3.1). The NSEC validator did not check for this case and accepted an NXDOMAIN response backed by such a record as secure.

The response code is not covered by any signature. An attacker who can modify DNS responses can take a genuine signed NODATA response for an empty non-terminal, change its response code to NXDOMAIN, and have the validator accept that an existing name does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix rejects NXDOMAIN as bogus, and validates NODATA as secure, when the covering NSEC record's next domain name is below the queried name and is not the zone apex. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: NSEC3 records from another zone were accepted in proofs of nonexistence
advisory.description:
When DNSSEC validation used NSEC3 records to prove that a name or record type does not exist, it compared only the hashed first label of each NSEC3 owner name with the hash of the name being checked. The rest of the owner name, which says which zone the record belongs to, was not checked.

Someone who controls any DNSSEC-signed zone can publish a signed NSEC3 record whose first label is the hash of a name in another zone. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can then use it to make the validator accept that the name in the other zone does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix requires a matching NSEC3 record to belong to a zone that contains the checked name, and ignores NSEC3 records whose owner is not directly below the RRSIG signer name. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Parent-side NSEC at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence below the cut
advisory.description:
At a delegation, the parent zone signs an NSEC record for the child's name whose type bitmap has NS but not SOA (or has DNAME). RFC 6840 section 4.1 says such a record only proves that no DS record exists at that name. It says nothing about names below the cut or about other types at the cut, because those belong to the child zone.

DNSSEC validation did not make this distinction. It used such a record as a covering NSEC for names below the cut, and as a direct match proving that other types did not exist at the cut. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay the parent's genuine signed records to get an NXDOMAIN or NODATA response for an existing name in the child zone accepted as secure. A recursor caches that denial for the negative TTL.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix adds `NSEC::is_ancestor_delegation()` in hickory-proto. Validation no longer uses such a record to cover a name below its owner, and treats a direct match on it as bogus unless the query is for DS. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: DNSSEC validation cache could reuse an Insecure result for a different name
advisory.description:
The DNSSEC validation cache used a 64-bit hash of the query as its key, and two keys with the same hash counted as equal. The `Hash` implementation of `Name` hashed the bytes of the labels but not where one label ends and the next begins, so names that differ only in the placement of dots (such as `ab.c.` and `a.bc.`) hashed to the same value.

An attacker who controls an unsigned delegation whose name collides in this way with a name in a signed zone can first get an Insecure result cached for their own name. A forged response for the signed name is then served from that cache entry without signature checks and returned with the AD bit clear, where validation should have failed.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix stores the query in the cache key and compares it on lookup. The `Hash` implementations of `Label`, `Name` and `LowerName` in hickory-proto were also changed to include label boundaries. Both are in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: NSEC wraparound detection trusted an unvalidated SOA record
advisory.description:
The last NSEC record in a zone points back to the zone apex. To recognise it, DNSSEC validation treated an NSEC record as covering every name after its owner when its next domain name equalled the owner name of an SOA record in the response. That SOA record did not have to pass validation.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay a genuine NSEC record and its RRSIG, add a forged SOA record whose name equals that NSEC record's next domain name, and so make the validator accept that any name sorting after the NSEC owner does not exist.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix recognises a wraparound NSEC record from the chain itself (its next domain name sorts at or before its owner and is the zone of the queried name) and only uses validated SOA records. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Spoofed malformed UDP datagrams abort DNS lookups
advisory.description:
While waiting for a reply on a UDP connection, the client parsed every datagram that arrived from the name server's address and port before checking its message ID. If parsing failed, the attempt ended with an error instead of dropping the datagram and waiting for the real reply. The receive loop also gave up after three datagrams.

An off-path attacker who can guess the client's source port, but not the transaction ID, can send one malformed datagram with a spoofed source address and make the pending lookup fail.

The fix reads the message ID from the first two bytes before parsing, ignores short datagrams and datagrams with the wrong ID, keeps listening until the outer timeout, and only then parses the response. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: RRSIG signer name was not checked against the zone of the signed records
advisory.description:
DNSSEC validation checked an RRset against the DNSKEYs of whatever zone was named in the RRSIG's Signer's Name field. RFC 4035 section 5.3.1 requires that name to be the zone that contains the RRset, but this was not checked.

Anyone who controls a DNSSEC-signed zone, and can answer or modify DNS responses, can therefore sign records for names in an unrelated zone with their own keys and have the validator accept them as secure.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` (resolver, recursor and client) when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix ignores an RRSIG whose signer name is not the RRset's owner name or one of its ancestors. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Inverted NSEC3 comparison lets one record "prove" that almost any name does not exist
advisory.description:
When DNSSEC validation looks for the NSEC3 record that covers a hashed name, the last record in the zone's hash chain needs special handling, because its next hashed owner name sorts before its own hash. For that record the two comparisons were reversed: it was treated as covering every hash below its owner hash or above its next hash, which is mostly the part of the chain it does not cover.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay that one signed NSEC3 record, with its RRSIG, from the target zone and use it in forged negative answers. The validator then accepts proof that names which do exist have no records.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` (resolver, recursor and client) when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`. The same code was in hickory-proto before it moved to hickory-net.

The fix corrects the comparison in `find_covering_record`. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Child-side NSEC or NSEC3 record accepted as proof that a delegation has no DS record
advisory.description:
To show that a delegation is insecure, a validator needs proof that the parent zone has no DS record for it. That proof must come from the parent side of the zone cut: RFC 4035 section 5.2, RFC 5155 section 8.9 and RFC 6840 section 4.4 require the matching NSEC or NSEC3 record not to have the SOA bit set, since a record with SOA comes from the child zone's apex.

DNSSEC validation did not check this. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can answer a DS query with the child zone's own signed NSEC or NSEC3 record for its apex, which does not list DS, and have the validator accept that the delegation is insecure. Records in the child zone can then be forged without any signature.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix treats a NODATA proof for a DS query as bogus when the directly matching NSEC or NSEC3 record has SOA in its type bitmap. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Parent-side NSEC3 at a zone cut accepted as proof of nonexistence at and below the cut
advisory.description:
At a delegation, the parent zone signs an NSEC3 record for the child's name whose type bitmap has NS but not SOA (or has DNAME). RFC 6840 section 4.1 and RFC 5155 section 8.3 say such a record only proves that no DS record exists at that name.

NSEC3 validation picked the closest encloser by matching the hashed owner name alone, without looking at the type bitmap, so it accepted such a record as the closest encloser for names below the cut. For NODATA responses, it accepted a direct match on such a record as proof that any type other than the queried one and CNAME was absent, not only DS. An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can replay the parent's genuine signed records to get an NXDOMAIN for a name below the cut, or a NODATA for a non-DS type at the cut, accepted as secure. A recursor caches that denial for the negative TTL.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix adds `NSEC3::is_ancestor_delegation()` in hickory-proto. Validation no longer accepts such a record as a closest encloser, and treats a direct match on it as bogus unless the query is for DS. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: DNSSEC validation accepted a validly signed but unrelated RRset as the answer
advisory.description:
When a response had a non-empty answer section, DNSSEC validation treated it as a positive answer as long as the records in it validated. It did not check that any of those records had the queried name and either the queried type or type CNAME.

An attacker who can answer or modify DNS responses can therefore return a genuine, signed RRset for some other name or type, and have it accepted as a validated answer to the query instead of being handled as a response with no matching data.

This affects DNSSEC validation through `DnssecDnsHandle` when built with `dnssec-ring` or `dnssec-aws-lc-rs`.

The fix requires at least one answer record that matches the query name and is either of the queried type or a CNAME, both for positive responses and when NSEC records are checked. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Zone file lexer panics on a token of 4096 or more characters
advisory.description:
The zone file lexer read each token in a loop capped at 4,096 iterations, with an `assert!` on the loop counter as a safety bound. A single token long enough to reach that bound, for example a very long name or character string in a zone file, triggered the assertion and the parser panicked instead of returning the token or an error.

Code that parses zone files from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service.

The fix removes the iteration bound, so the lexer ends only when it reaches the end of a token or an error. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Memory amplification from record counts in the DNS message header
advisory.description:
When a DNS message is decoded, the vectors for the question, answer, authority and additional sections were created with `Vec::with_capacity` set to the counts in the message header. Those counts come from the sender and are not checked against the size of the message, so a single small packet that claims 65,535 records makes the decoder reserve memory for that many records (about 18 MB, according to the upstream advisory) before it reads any record and fails.

Any code that decodes untrusted DNS messages is exposed. That includes servers, and clients and resolvers that receive spoofed responses. Repeated packets can drive memory use up and cause a denial of service.

The fix caps the initial capacity at 8 entries and lets the vectors grow as records are actually decoded. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Panic on a malformed `alpn` value when parsing SVCB or HTTPS records from text
advisory.description:
When an SVCB or HTTPS record is parsed from its text (zone file) form, the `alpn` service parameter value is split into a list of protocol names. That step called `expect` on the result, on the assumption that it could not fail. A malformed value, such as one with an unbalanced quote (`alpn="h`), two commas in a row or an invalid escape, makes it fail, so the parser panicked instead of returning an error.

Code that parses zone files or record text from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service. Records decoded from the DNS wire format are not parsed this way.

The fix returns a parse error instead. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Integer underflow when reporting a malformed TSIG record
advisory.description:
When a TSIG record is decoded from the DNS wire format, its MAC length and "other data" length are checked against the end of the record data. If a check failed, the error value was built from `end_idx - decoder.index()`. For a malformed record the decoder can already be past `end_idx`, so this unsigned subtraction underflows.

In builds with overflow checks enabled (the `dev` profile by default) the underflow panics, so a peer that sends a crafted TSIG record can crash the process. In builds without overflow checks the result wraps and is only used in the returned error.

The fix returns a plain "insufficient bytes" error without the subtraction. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Panic when an SVCB or HTTPS parameter value is a single quote character
advisory.description:
When an SVCB or HTTPS record is parsed from its text (zone file) form, surrounding double quotes are removed from each service parameter value by checking that the value starts and ends with `"` and slicing off the first and last character. A value that is a single `"` (for example `alpn="`) passes that check, and the slice `[1..0]` panics.

Code that parses zone files or record text from an untrusted source can be made to panic, which is a denial of service. Records decoded from the DNS wire format are not parsed this way.

The fix rejects a lone quote character with a parse error before the slice. It is in 0.26.2.

advisory.title: Unbounded retries on truncated responses in the name server pool
advisory.description:
When an upstream answer had the TC (truncated) bit set, the resolver's name server pool disabled UDP and sent the query again. It did this for every truncated answer, including answers that already came over TCP, and it kept no count of retries.

A name server that sets TC on every answer, which anyone running an authoritative server the resolver queries can do, kept each lookup re-sending queries over the same connection until the request deadline (5 seconds by default) ran out. This uses up resolver resources and sends many queries per lookup.

From 0.26.2 a truncated answer received after UDP has already been disabled ends the lookup with `NetError::Truncated` instead of retrying again.

advisory.title: Recursor kept querying cyclic glueless sibling delegations
advisory.description:
Two zones can each delegate to name servers named only inside the other zone, with no glue records (the cyclic sibling case in RFC 9471 section 2.3). Such delegations can never be resolved, but the recursor did not stop when it came back to a zone it was already resolving. It kept sending queries until the per-request limits ran out, and zero TTLs on the referral NS records made this worse.

Someone who controls two such zones can make a recursor send many upstream queries for each client query.

This affects the recursive resolver, which is in hickory-resolver behind the opt-in `recursor` feature from 0.26.0-beta.1. Earlier releases shipped it as the separate hickory-recursor crate.

From 0.26.2 each client request tracks the zones on its resolution stack and refuses to enter a zone that is already on it.

advisory.title: Recursor followed every glueless name server in a referral, with no per-query budget
advisory.description:
When a referral listed name servers outside the delegated zone and gave no glue addresses, the recursor looked up A and AAAA records for every listed name server, recursing into each one. Only the chain-depth limits applied. There was no cap on how many name servers it chased per referral or on the total upstream work per client query.

Someone who controls a zone can return referrals that list many glueless name servers in a victim's domain, and nest them, so that each client query makes the recursor send a large number of queries to the victim's servers (the NXNSAttack pattern). The same can exhaust the recursor's own resources.

This affects the recursive resolver, which is in hickory-resolver behind the opt-in `recursor` feature from 0.26.0-beta.1. Earlier releases shipped it as the separate hickory-recursor crate.

From 0.26.2 the recursor follows at most 5 glueless name servers per delegation and sends at most 200 upstream queries per client request.

advisory.title: `Resolver::lookup` and `lookup_ip` returned records that failed DNSSEC validation
advisory.description:
With DNSSEC validation enabled, `Resolver::lookup()` and `Resolver::lookup_ip()` returned `Ok` with the records even when validation found the response bogus. The result was only visible in each record's proof status, which callers had to inspect themselves.

Applications that enable validation and treat a successful lookup as validated data would therefore accept forged or tampered answers from anyone who can answer or modify their DNS traffic.

From 0.26.2 a lookup whose records are bogus fails with a "DNSSEC validation failed" error (`DnsError::DnssecBogus`), the error is not retried, and the hickory-server forwarder answers SERVFAIL for it.

advisory.title: `libsqlite3-sys` via C SQLite CVE-2026-119375
advisory.description:
SQLite versions before 3.54.0 can return uninitialized page-cache memory when a process opens a database file together with a sibling write-ahead-log (`-wal`) file whose page size differs from the database's. A crafted pair of files can make ordinary queries return stale bytes from the process's memory. The attack vector is local and needs the victim to open the files.

As `libsqlite3-sys` bundles SQLite when it is built from its bundled source (the `bundled` feature, which `rusqlite`'s `bundled` feature enables), it is susceptible to the vulnerability. The releases `0.6.0` to `0.38.2` bundle SQLite `3.13.0` to `3.53.2` and are affected; the earlier releases contain no SQLite source. `libsqlite3-sys` was updated to bundle the patched version of SQLite in `0.39.0` (SQLite `3.54.0`) and `0.39.1` (SQLite `3.54.1`), released with [`rusqlite` 0.41](https://github.com/rusqlite/rusqlite/releases/tag/v0.41.0). `libsqlite3-sys` `0.39` declares Rust 1.88 and `rusqlite` `0.41` declares Rust 1.89.

Only a process that opens a database file, with its `-wal`, that a less trusted party could have written is exposed. A build that links a system SQLite instead of the bundled source is not affected by the copy in this crate; its exposure is that of the system library's version. The `bundled-sqlcipher` feature builds SQLCipher instead of SQLite; in `0.39.0` and `0.39.1` it depends on `sqlcipher-src =419.0.6`, which bundles SQLite `3.53.4` and is affected.

advisory.title: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
advisory.description:
`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

advisory.title: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
advisory.description:
`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

advisory.title: Zero-length DATAGRAM frames bypass the receive buffer limit in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
quinn-proto bounds its queue of received datagrams by charging each queued frame's payload length
against `TransportConfig::datagram_receive_buffer_size`, evicting the oldest datagrams when the
limit is exceeded. A DATAGRAM frame with an empty payload was charged zero bytes, so it never
triggered eviction and was appended to the queue, which has no other bound.

DATAGRAM frames are not subject to flow control. A peer that has completed the handshake can
therefore send a stream of empty DATAGRAM frames and grow the receiver's heap without limit until
the process is killed. An application that reads incoming datagrams but does so more slowly than
the peer sends them is still affected. Receiving datagrams is enabled by default, so all endpoints
that do not explicitly set `datagram_receive_buffer_size(None)` are affected.

The send path had the same accounting flaw: an application could enqueue an unbounded number of
empty outgoing datagrams without ever receiving `SendDatagramError::Blocked`.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by accounting for the fixed per-datagram overhead in both
directions, so that every queued datagram consumes buffer space.

Thanks to [@alexpyattaev](https://github.com/alexpyattaev) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Unbounded growth of pending connection ID retirements in quinn-proto
advisory.description:
When processing a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame, quinn-proto queues a RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frame for
each connection ID that the peer asked it to retire. The normal path bounds this queue and closes
the connection with a CONNECTION_ID_LIMIT_ERROR if the bound would be exceeded. However, the path
handling a connection ID that had already been retired pushed onto the queue without applying
the limit and without deduplicating.

A peer that has completed the handshake can first send a NEW_CONNECTION_ID frame with a large
`retire_prior_to` value to advance the receiver's connection ID window, and then repeatedly send
NEW_CONNECTION_ID frames with sequence numbers below that window. Each such frame adds another
entry to the queue. The queue is only drained by sending RETIRE_CONNECTION_ID frames, which are
subject to congestion control, so a peer that withholds acknowledgements can stall the drain while
continuing to flood, growing the victim's memory use without bound.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.17 by applying the same limit on the already-retired path.

Thanks to [@scadastrangelove](https://github.com/scadastrangelove) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: MAX_STREAM_DATA frame can open streams beyond the stream limit
advisory.description:
When a MAX_STREAM_DATA frame named a peer-initiated bidirectional stream that was not open yet, `received_max_stream_data` treated the stream, and every lower-numbered stream, as opened without checking the stream ID against the limit advertised to the peer. RFC 9000 section 4.6 requires closing the connection with `STREAM_LIMIT_ERROR` in this case, and the STREAM and RESET_STREAM handlers already did so.

After the handshake, a peer can send one small MAX_STREAM_DATA frame naming a very large stream index, and `accept` then yields every stream up to that index. In `quinn`, a loop that keeps calling `accept_bi` can be handed more than 2^40 streams. Depending on the runtime, the endpoint runs out of memory, stops accepting new connections, or keeps busy indefinitely, even after the peer has gone away. Clients and servers that accept peer-initiated bidirectional streams are affected. Unidirectional streams are not.

The fix validates the stream ID in `received_max_stream_data` and adds a defensive check where streams are opened implicitly. It is in 0.11.19.

advisory.title: Remote peer can panic quinn-proto with zero-length STREAM frames during unordered reads
advisory.description:
When a stream is read in unordered mode (for example through `RecvStream::read(false)` in
quinn-proto or `read_unordered` in `quinn`), quinn-proto proactively deduplicates received data
by recording received ranges in a `RangeSet` through its `replace` method. When an incoming
STREAM frame carried an empty payload, the `Drop` implementation of the iterator returned by
`replace` inserted an empty range into the set, violating the invariant that stored ranges are
non-empty. Subsequent frames overlapping that region then caused a panic while processing the
stream.

A remote peer can trigger this with five small STREAM frames (two of them zero-length) once the
application has put the stream in unordered-read mode. The default ordered read path is not
affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by ignoring empty ranges in `RangeSet::replace`.

Thanks to Otto Hermann ([@ojhermann](https://github.com/ojhermann)) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Long Retry token can panic or exhaust memory in a QUIC client
advisory.description:
A client kept the token from a Retry packet without any length limit and put it into the header of every Initial packet it sent afterwards. Initial datagrams are 1200 bytes. When the token and connection IDs left no room for the minimum payload, `PacketBuilder::new` computed a minimum packet size larger than the maximum, which only a debug assertion checked. On the next `poll_transmit`, debug builds panic, and release builds try to allocate more than 10 GiB in one call. With longer tokens the allocation fails and the process aborts.

A matching Retry packet can be built from the client's first Initial alone. The attacker can therefore be the server being contacted, or anyone who sees that Initial and can answer before the server does. Every application that makes outgoing connections with `quinn-proto` is affected, including all `quinn` clients. Servers do not process Retry packets.

The fix closes the connection with `PROTOCOL_VIOLATION` when an Initial token leaves too little room for frames. That covers Retry tokens and cached address-validation tokens, since both come from the peer. It also reserves room for CONNECTION_CLOSE after large Initial headers. Both changes are in 0.11.19.

advisory.title: Peer minimum ACK delay can panic quinn-proto when ACK_FREQUENCY transmission is enabled
advisory.description:
When sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is enabled through
`TransportConfig::ack_frequency_config(Some(..))`, the peer's transport parameters could cause
`AckFrequencyState::candidate_max_ack_delay` to call `Duration::clamp` with a minimum greater
than its maximum, which panics.

For example, a peer advertising a `min_ack_delay` of 100,000 microseconds and a `max_ack_delay`
of 100 milliseconds passes transport parameter validation. At a 5 ms RTT, the lower bound of the
clamp becomes 100 ms while the upper bound is 25 ms, violating the precondition of `clamp` and
panicking while driving the connection. Both automatically derived and explicitly configured
maximum ACK delays use this calculation.

Sending ACK_FREQUENCY frames is disabled by default, so only endpoints that opt in are affected.

The flaw was corrected in 0.11.18 by computing the delay with explicit minimum and maximum bounds
instead of `clamp`.

Thanks to [@zerox80](https://github.com/zerox80) for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Remote memory exhaustion in quinn-proto from unbounded out-of-order stream reassembly
advisory.description:
The `Assembler` component that assembles unordered stream fragments into consecutive chunks of the
stream incurs some overhead for non-contiguous fragments. Readers that read from a RecvStream in
order (through an `AsyncRead` impl for example) will be sensitive to peers that send fragments
while leaving out early parts of the stream, and in particular, fragments with many gaps (because
these cannot be defragmented). In such a scenario, the receiving connection suffers from high
buffer overhead, enabling memory exhaustion.

advisory.title: Receive loop can spin after a truncated datagram
advisory.description:
Some targets read one datagram per `recvmsg` call instead of using `recvmmsg`: Apple platforms without the `fast-apple-datapath` feature, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Solaris and illumos, and from 0.6 also DragonFly BSD, Redox and GNU/Hurd. On these targets the receive loop set up its `msghdr` only once and looked at the `MSG_TRUNC` flag before checking whether `recvmsg` had failed. After a datagram larger than the receive buffer was dropped, a following `EAGAIN` still saw the old truncation flag. The loop then kept issuing non-blocking receives instead of returning `WouldBlock`.

When the receive buffer is smaller than a datagram that arrives, a remote sender can keep the task that drives the socket busy, before any QUIC packet authentication. The loop ends only when a later datagram fits in the buffer. Whether an application is exposed therefore depends on the receive buffer size it uses. Linux, Android, FreeBSD and Windows use other receive paths and are not affected.

The fix rebuilds the header before every `recvmsg` call and returns receive errors before checking the truncation flag. It is in 0.5.16 and 0.6.3.

advisory.title: Insufficient archive validation can cause out-of-bounds reads in archives containing Rc/Arc
advisory.description:
Shared pointer validation keyed already-validated pointees by their address and
type, but did not include pointer metadata. For unsized pointees, an archive
could therefore contain multiple `Rc`, `Arc`, or weak pointers that shared a
data address but used different metadata, such as different slice lengths.

Once the first pointer had been validated, later pointers to the same address
skipped pointee validation. The safe checked `rkyv::access` API could
consequently return a slice with a forged length, allowing safe indexing to
read out of bounds. The same validation bypass was reachable through checked
deserialization with `rkyv::from_bytes`.

Version 0.8.17 includes pointer metadata in shared pointer validation and
rejects conflicting metadata. The 0.7 series is also affected but is no
longer supported by upstream. Users who process untrusted archives should upgrade
to 0.8.17 or later.

advisory.title: Marvin Attack: potential key recovery through timing sidechannels
advisory.description:
### Impact
Due to a non-constant-time implementation, information about the private key is leaked through timing information which is observable over the network. An attacker may be able to use that information to recover the key.

### Patches
The `rsa` v0.10 series includes a migration to `crypto-bigint` and constant-time mitigations recommended in `draft-irtf-cfrg-rsa-guidance`. Upgrading to this release should resolve all known constant-time issues.

### References
This vulnerability was discovered as part of the "[Marvin Attack]", which revealed several implementations of RSA including OpenSSL had not properly mitigated timing sidechannel attacks.

[Marvin Attack]: https://people.redhat.com/~hkario/marvin/

advisory.title: Unbounded 32-bit allocation
advisory.description:
Both the SSH agent server and client accepted peer-controlled frame lengths
without enforcing a maximum frame size. This could cause large memory
allocations while parsing a maliciously crafted agent frame.

A malicious peer could advertise an oversized frame length, causing the client
or server to attempt a large memory allocation before validating the frame,
potentially leading to memory exhaustion or process termination.

This is fixed by enforcing a maximum agent frame size of 256 KiB and
rejecting oversized frames before buffer allocation.

advisory.title: SSH message fields allocated before their size is checked
advisory.description:
Many of russh's client and server message handlers decoded length-prefixed strings, byte fields and name-lists from the peer into owned `String`, `Vec` or name-list values first and only checked their size and meaning afterwards. This includes the algorithm name-lists in `SSH_MSG_KEXINIT`, which a server parses during the initial key exchange, before any authentication.

A peer can fill these fields with oversized or highly fragmented values, for example a name-list of hundreds of thousands of one-letter algorithm names, and make russh allocate far more memory than the packet itself takes. With many concurrent connections this can exhaust the memory of a server process.

From 0.61.0, name-lists are rejected before they are split into separate strings when they are longer than 16 KiB or hold more than 1,024 entries, and the key exchange decodes its algorithm lists through this bounded decoder.

advisory.title: Client `Handler` callbacks run for channels the client never opened
advisory.description:
On the client side, russh passed channel messages from the server (data, extended data, EOF, close, success, failure, open failure and the exit-status, exit-signal and xon-xoff requests) to the application's `client::Handler` callbacks without checking that the channel number belonged to a channel the client had opened and the server had confirmed. The server side already performed this check.

A malicious or compromised SSH server can therefore send these messages for any channel number, including the next number the client will allocate (they are assigned in order) or one it has already closed. An application that tracks per-channel state can be made to record a false exit status, see a channel close before its real output arrives, or panic when it looks up a channel it does not know.

From 0.63.1 the client ignores channel messages for channels that are not established and confirmed, and handles an open failure only for a channel it is actually opening.

advisory.title: Pre-authentication allocation from the keyboard-interactive response count
advisory.description:
A server that answers a keyboard-interactive authentication request with prompts (`Auth::Partial`, as a TOTP or other second-factor login does) then parses the client's `SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_INFO_RESPONSE`. russh read the number of responses from that message and reserved a vector of that many entries before reading any of them. A client that has not authenticated can send a very large count in a packet that carries no responses at all, and the server tries to allocate several gigabytes and may be killed for running out of memory.

Servers whose handler keeps the default behaviour, which rejects keyboard-interactive authentication, are not affected. From 0.60.1 the count is limited by how many responses the remaining packet data could actually hold.

advisory.title: No limit on the size of a decompressed SSH packet
advisory.description:
With `zlib` or `zlib@openssh.com` compression negotiated, the packet length that russh checks applies to the compressed payload only. The decompressor kept growing its output buffer until the whole payload was inflated, with no limit of its own, so a packet that is small on the wire could expand to hundreds of megabytes before it was parsed.

The default server configuration offers both zlib methods, and a client that lists compression first can select it during the initial key exchange. That client can then send such a packet after `NEWKEYS` but before authenticating, so a russh server with default settings can be made to use large amounts of memory by an unauthenticated peer. A malicious server can do the same to a client that negotiated compression.

From 0.61.1, decompressed output is capped at the same maximum as an uncompressed packet (256 KiB plus a few bytes of header room), and larger packets are rejected with `Error::PacketSize`.

advisory.title: Unchecked `CryptoVec` allocation and growth handling
advisory.description:
`CryptoVec` used unchecked capacity growth, unchecked length arithmetic, and
unsafe allocation and locking paths. In affected `russh` releases,
attacker-controlled input could reach these code paths through buffer resizing
operations.

Two affected reachability paths were identified:

* **Current `russh` releases (`0.60.x` before the fix)**
  Local SSH agent peers could provide attacker-controlled frame lengths that
  were used to resize internal buffers before validation in:

  * `AgentClient::read_response`
  * `agent::server::Connection::run`

* **Historical `russh` releases before `0.58.0`**
  `CryptoVec` was also used for non-secret transport and compression buffers,
  allowing remote SSH traffic to trigger `CryptoVec` growth through:

  * transport packet reads
  * zlib decompression output

These remote paths were removed in `0.58.0` when `CryptoVec` stopped being used
for those buffers.

Under constrained memory conditions, historical `russh` versions prior to
`0.58.0` can abort the process when remote compressed payload expansion causes
allocation failure in `CryptoVec`. This was reproduced through the compression
path and resulted in process termination in the Unix allocation/locking
implementation after null pointer allocation failure.

For current affected releases, oversized local SSH agent frame lengths could
trigger untrusted-input-driven buffer growth prior to validation.

No practical remote code execution, integrity or confidentiality impact has
been demonstrated.

Fixed by validating CryptoVec growth operations and rejecting oversized SSH
agent frame lengths before buffer allocation.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos
to that server name.

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that
name carry only an X25519 key share, while `supported_groups` still lists
X25519MLKEM768 first. If the genuine server accepts that share rather than
sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake
completes with classical-only key exchange and no error. This persists for as
long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections
("harvest now, decrypt later"). There is no key compromise and no
authentication bypass.

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and
- other server names.

This behaviour is discussed in
[draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations),
so the practical impact depends largely on server policy.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries
advisory.description:
Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level
when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. For example,
a plaintext `EncryptedExtensions` message packed into the same record as the
`ServerHello` was accepted.

RFC 8446 section 5.1 requires that handshake messages do not span key changes,
and that implementations terminate the connection with an "unexpected_message"
alert if they do.

The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker
cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that
a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext
without rustls rejecting the connection.

This is functionally the same bug as Go's
[GO-2026-4340](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-4340) (CVE-2025-61730).

advisory.title: Brotli certificate decompression can allocate up to 1 GiB before authentication
advisory.description:
The built-in Brotli certificate decompressor (enabled by the non-default
`brotli` crate feature) bounded the size of the decompressed output, but
accepted a peer-selected history window. Brotli's large-window extension was
enabled, so a five-byte header could cause an allocation of 1 GiB. A peer can
abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request.

No trusted certificate is required by the attacker. Affected configurations are:

- clients that enable the `brotli` feature and connect to a malicious server, and
- servers that enable the `brotli` feature and request client certificates.

Applications that do not enable the `brotli` feature are not affected.

advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that

sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake

long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and

advisory.title: Reachable panic in certificate revocation list parsing
advisory.description:
A panic was reachable when parsing certificate revocation lists via [`BorrowedCertRevocationList::from_der`]
or [`OwnedCertRevocationList::from_der`].  This was the result of mishandling a syntactically valid empty
`BIT STRING` appearing in the `onlySomeReasons` element of a `IssuingDistributionPoint` CRL extension.

This panic is reachable prior to a CRL's signature being verified.

Applications that do not use CRLs are not affected.

Thank you to [@tynus3](https://github.com/tynus3) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints for URI names were incorrectly accepted
advisory.description:
Name constraints for URI names were ignored and therefore accepted.

Note this library does not provide an API for asserting URI names, and URI name constraints are otherwise not implemented.  URI name constraints are now rejected unconditionally.

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name
advisory.description:
Permitted subtree name constraints for DNS names were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name.

This was incorrect because, given a name constraint of `accept.example.com`, `*.example.com` could feasibly allow a name of `reject.example.com` which is outside the constraint.
This is very similar to [CVE-2025-61727](https://go.dev/issue/76442).

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

The `webpki-roots` 0.26.11 compatibility package contains no independent trust
store and re-exports the roots from its separately resolved 1.x dependency.
That parent dependency must resolve to 1.0.10 or newer; an older parent remains
affected by this advisory.

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` aborts the process on a symlink entry with a large declared size
advisory.description:
`ZipArchive::extract()` sizes the symlink-target buffer from the uncompressed
size declared in the central directory record, before reading a single byte of
entry data:

```rust
let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize);
```

Both inputs are attacker-controlled. `ZipFile::size()` returns
`uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory, widened to a full `u64`
by a ZIP64 extended-information extra field, and is never cross-checked against
the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate
bound for a symlink target. `ZipFile::is_symlink()` is decided entirely by the
`S_IFLNK` bit of the external-attributes field.

`Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: when the reservation is refused it calls
`handle_alloc_error()` and aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic. It is
not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not
contained by running the call on a worker thread.

A 112-byte archive is sufficient. One `Stored` entry flagged `S_IFLNK` with a
ZIP64 field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62` and a zero-byte payload makes
`extract()` fail with:

```
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The declared value only needs to exceed the host's address space, not its RAM:
`Vec::with_capacity()` maps address space without touching pages, so resident
memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself. Under
a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far
enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices.

Applications that extract archives from untrusted input are affected on Unix and
Windows targets with default features and no special configuration: upload
handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup
restore and container-image layer extraction. No confidentiality or integrity
property is affected: there is no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no
disclosure and no data corruption.

The fix landed in [zip-rs/zip2#984](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/pull/984) and
shipped in 9.0.0.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3

advisory.title: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation
advisory.description:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory
advisory.description:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Error::downcast_mut()`
`event-listener` allows `!Send` tags to cross thread boundaries via `StackSlot`
advisory.description:
Affected versions of `event-listener` unconditionally implement `Send` and
`Sync` for `StackSlot<'_, T>`, the stack-allocated listener type created
by the `listener!` macro.

This allows a `!Send` tag type set via `Event::with_tag` to be moved to
another thread and accessed via `StackSlot::wait`, causing a data race in safe
code.

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Iterator` and `DoubleEndedIterator` impls for `glib::VariantStrIter`
advisory.description:
The `VariantStrIter::impl_get` function (called internally by implementations of the `Iterator` and `DoubleEndedIterator` traits for this type) was unsound, resulting in undefined behaviour.

An immutable reference `&p` to a `*mut libc::c_char` pointer initialized to `NULL` was passed as an argument to a C function that that mutates the pointer behind `&p` in-place (i.e. as an out-argument), which was unsound. After changes in recent versions of the Rust compiler, these unsound writes through `&p` now seem to be completely disregarded when building the `glib` crate with optimizations.

This subsequently caused all calls of `VariantStrIter::impl_get` to violate the safety requirements of the `std::ffi::CStr::from_ptr` function - which requires its argument to be a valid pointer to a C-style string - resulting in crashes due to `NULL` pointer dereferences.

This was fixed by passing the out-argument pointer explitly as `&mut p` instead of `&p`.

This issue has been present since this code was initially added in `glib` v0.15.0. The mismatch in mutability was likely missed (and not raised as an error by the compiler) because the C function wrapped by `VariantStrIter::impl_get` is variadic (`glib_sys::g_variant_get_child`), and the pointer in question is one of the variadic arguments.

advisory.title: xattr functions mark unwritten bytes as initialized when given a zero-length buffer
advisory.description:
The extended-attribute functions in `rustix::fs` (`getxattr`, `lgetxattr`, `fgetxattr`, `listxattr`, `llistxattr` and `flistxattr`) write into a `Buffer` and then mark as many bytes initialized as the system call reported. When the buffer has zero length, the operating system treats the call as a size query: it writes nothing and returns the size of the attribute value or of the name list. rustix still marked that many bytes as initialized.

Passing a `Vec` whose length equals its capacity through `spare_capacity` gives such a zero-length buffer, and rustix then set the vector's length past its capacity over memory that was never written. This is undefined behavior reachable from safe code. With an empty `&mut [MaybeUninit<u8>]` the call panics instead.

From 1.1.6 these functions return an empty result for a zero-length buffer, and new `getxattr_query`, `lgetxattr_query`, `fgetxattr_query`, `listxattr_query`, `llistxattr_query` and `flistxattr_query` functions return the size. The 0.38 series did not have the `Buffer` API and is not affected.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.
